n: Burden, or threat. (Worthington) --- Septuagint, "assumption," (Haydock) when the prophet saw in spirit the impending ruin. (Theodoret) --- Allegorically, Nahum is "the comforter" of the just, shewing that God will avenge their cause against Ninive, "the beautiful," and destroy the world, (kosmos, which also means "beautiful,") after which the saints shall reign in eternal glory. (Worthington) --- We have described Ninive, Jonas i. (Calmet) --- It was overturned first in the year of the world 3257, and again in the year 3378. (Usher) --- Elcesite. Some think that Elcesai was the father of Nahum; but most suppose that it was a village Galilee. (Calmet)
The Lord. The six following verses (Haydock) tend to excite attention. (Calmet)

Cleanse. Literally, "cleansing, he will not make innocent." (Haydock) --- The same expression is rendered, No man of himself is innocent before thee, Exodus xxxiv. 7. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "the innocent he will not deem innocent." (Haydock) --- No man is perfect in God’s sight, (Calmet) though they may appear to be such to others. (Haydock) --- None can escape punishment, if he be treated with rigour. De Dieu translates, "he will not utterly evacuate," or destroy, which seems very correct, Jeremias xxx. 11., and Numbers xiv. 18. --- Dust. He walks upon them as we do on dry land.
Desert, as at the Red Sea, Psalm cv. 9. --- Languisheth. The most fruitful places produce nothing, when God is angry.
Made. Septuagint, "shaken." --- Quaked. Hebrew and Septuagint, "risen." (Calmet)
Like fire. Septuagint, "melts kingdoms."
Hope. Septuagint, "fear." He approves of his faithful servants. (Haydock)

Thereof; viz. of Ninive. (Challoner) --- This is connected with Ver. 1. (Haydock) --- Ninive was taken by the waters of the Tigris overflowing, at the first siege. (Diod. ii.; Athen. xii.) --- The like might happen at the second, though profane authors be silent. (Calmet) --- Many think that the flood means great armies, Isaias viii. 7. (Forer.; Vatable) --- Septuagint, "He will utterly destroy: those who rise up and his enemies, darkness," &c. (Haydock) --- Chaldean, The.[Theodotion?] and Aq.[Aquila?] adopt the same sense, but Symmachus, &c., agree with us. (Calmet)

Affliction. Septuagint add, "for the same thing, or together." (Haydock) --- Many hence infer, that those who have been slain by God, like the Sodomites, &c., will not be condemned to hell. (Origen, i. Ezec.; St. Jerome.; St. Thomas Aquinas, 3. p. q. 59. a. 5.) --- But this principle cannot be always correct. (Calmet) --- Their temporal suffering might usher in eternal ones. (St. Gregory, Mor. xviii. 12.) --- Ninive shall perish; so that a second blow will not be requisite, 1 Kings xxvi. 8. (Drusius) (Calmet)

Dry. The Assyrians, feasting in the hopes that they would speedily become masters of Jerusalem, were cut off in one night. (Worthington) --- God's enemies cannot escape; as when a thorn bush has taken fire, all must perish, Psalm lvii. 10., and Isaias ix. 18. (Calmet)

Forth. Some understand this of Sennacherib. But as his attempt against the people seems to have been prior to the prophecy of Nahum, we may better understand it of Holofernes. (Challoner) --- One. Septuagint, "a most wicked thought against the Lord, devising opposition." (Haydock) --- We may render, "hath come," &c., alluding to Sennacherib and Rabsaces, Isaias xxxvi. 18. and xxxvii. 23. (Calmet)

Perfect. That is, however strong or numerous their forces may be, they shall be cut off, and their prince or leader shall pass away and disappear. (Challoner) --- If there were many just at Ninive, or among the Jews, (Calmet) a moderate chastisement would suffice. (Haydock) --- The latter have been afflicted; now their enemies shall suffer. Septuagint have read otherwise: (Calmet) "the Lord, reigning over the great waters; thus shall they be divided, and thou shalt be heard of no more." (Haydock)
Asunder. Ezechias was tributary to Assyria, 4 Kings xviii. 14. After the fall of Ninive, its yoke was removed. (Calmet)

Commandment. That is, a decree concerning thee, O king of Ninive, thy seed shall fail, &c. (Challoner) --- His son Asarhaddon succeeded; but soon the line was extinct. (Worthington) --- No alarm shall be spread by thee. --- Grave. Sennacherib was slain in the temple: (Isaias xxxvii. 38.; Calmet) or the idols were deemed unclean by the victors. (Eurip.[Euripides?] Troad.) (Haydock)

Peace. Sentinels were established on the hills. --- Festivals. St. Jerome quotes the Book of Paralipomenon as saying (Calmet) that the Jews could not observe the Passover in the first month. But they did it in the second, after they knew that Sennacherib was slain, 2 Paralipomenon xxxii. (Haydock) --- This passage does not, however, appear at present in Scripture, and it could not speak of the second month (Calmet) following Nisan, (Haydock) as the king was slain forty-five days (Tobias i. 22.; Greek, 55.) after his return to Ninive; and some time must have elapsed before he could get thither, and the news arrive in Judea. (Calmet) --- Belial; the wicked one, viz. the Assyrian. (Challoner)

f: Commentary on Nahum

According to the Seventy translators, in the order of the twelve prophets Nahum is placed after Jonah, because they seem to prophesy about the same city. For it is written in Jonah: The word of the Lord came to Jonah, son of Amittai, saying: Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it. But in Nahum this is the opening: The taking up of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. Therefore both weave their prophecy about Nineveh, the metropolis of the Assyrians, which is now called Ninus. Moreover, in the Hebrew, Micah is placed after Jonah, and Micah is followed by Nahum, which means consoler. For the ten tribes had already been led away into captivity by the Assyrians under Hezekiah, king of Judah, under whom now also the vision against Nineveh is seen, for the consolation of the people carried away. Nor was it a small consolation, both for those who were already serving the Assyrians and for the rest, who under Hezekiah, of the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, were being besieged by the same enemies, to hear that the Assyrians too were to be taken by the Chaldeans, as will be shown in what follows in this book. But it must be understood — since Nineveh in our language, from the Hebrew, sounds beautiful; and this world is called beautiful, whence among the Greeks too κόσμος (world) received its name from adornment —, that whatever is now said against Nineveh is proclaimed figuratively of the world. For this reason the taking up, which the Seventy translate λῆμμα, and which Aquila translated ἄρμα, is given among the Hebrews as massa, that is, a heavy burden, because it presses down on her against whom it is seen, and does not allow her to raise her neck. Moreover, as to what is added, Nahum the Elkoshite, some think that Elkoshite was Nahum's father, and that according to the Hebrew tradition he too was a prophet, whereas Elkosh is to this day a hamlet in Galilee, small indeed, and scarcely showing in its ruins the traces of old buildings, but still known to the Jews, and pointed out to me as well by the man who was leading me around. At the same time this too must be noted, that this very taking up, or burden, or weight, is the prophet's vision. For he does not speak in ἐκστάσει (ecstasy), as Montanus and Prisca and Maximilla rave, but what he prophesies is the book of the vision of one who understands everything he speaks, and who makes the weight of the enemies a vision among his own people. Therefore, concerning the consummation of the world according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), O Paula and Eustochium, the prophecy is woven for the consolation of the saints, so that whatever they see in the world they may despise as passing and perishable, and may prepare themselves for the day of judgment, where the Lord is to be the avenger against the true Assyrians.
Commentary on Nahum

The burden of Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. First, he defines the purpose of the prophecy, and usefully clarifies what and where it looks to; then he makes clear who is speaking and from where. For he says "burden," that is, the prophecy that has been received and set forth and is at hand would be understood not about any others, but against Nineveh, or in other words, let the burden of the prophecy be understood as Nineveh. And the book is inscribed "The Vision of Nahum of Elkosh." This is doubtless a village somewhere in the land of the Jews. For we shall take 'of Elkosh' not as from a father, but rather as from a place. And we say this, having the tradition from the readings.
Commentary on Nahum

A jealous God, and an avenging Lord. The voice of the prophet praising God because he has avenged on the Assyrians the wrong done to his people. Or, according to a higher understanding, because he hears the groaning of his saints, and at the consummation of the world makes the adversaries feel punishments. That zeal is taken in a good sense, the apostle Paul too shows, saying: Be zealous for the greater gifts, and in another place: For I am zealous for you with the zeal of God, and the Lord himself in the psalm: The zeal of your house has consumed me, and Elijah: Zealous, he says, I have been zealous for the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel. We read also of the zeal of Phinehas, and of Mattathias. And Simon the Zealot, the apostle of Jesus Christ, whom Mark the evangelist calls Simon the Cananaean. But the Lord is zealous for the salvation of those over whom he is zealous, so that those whom his clemency could not save, his jealousy may save. Hence also to Jerusalem, which because of its excessive sins did not deserve the visitation of his zeal and fury, God speaks in Ezekiel: My zeal has departed from you, and I will be angry with you no more. So as long as the world was doing repentance, its consummation did not come about; but after iniquity was multiplied and the charity of many grew cold, so that even the elect of God are tempted, then the zealous Lord comes for vengeance, not that he himself is an enemy and avenger, which is said of the devil, but that his vengeance is hostile, and like fire consumes wood, hay and stubble, so that pure gold and silver may remain.

The Lord avenging, and having fury: the Lord avenging on his foes, and he himself angry with his enemies. LXX: The Lord avenging with fury, the Lord avenging on his adversaries, and he himself taking away his enemies. According to both understandings, because the Lord loves the one whom he rebukes, and chastises every son whom he receives, he is therefore angry, so that he may take away whatever is adverse and hostile to him, and so that, when the foes and the contrary thoughts are broken and their words taken away, they may return to their former state. Then in what follows he says: The Lord is patient, and his strength long. But since we have once undertaken to expound the history as well, let us understand the enemies and foes of God to be the Assyrians, against whom, though he has long been patient, he will afterwards show himself an avenger with fury and wrath.
Commentary on Nahum

God is jealous and the Lord avenges; the Lord avenges with wrath; the Lord avenges his adversaries, and he cuts off his enemies. The Lord is long-suffering and his strength is great, and he will by no means clear the guilty. The saying is profound, and not easy to grasp, except only for those who are willing to examine closely the things in it. And if it should be understood as having been directed to the Jews, we will find the exhortation suitably mixed with moderate rebuke. But if someone should think it was made and spoken against Nineveh, the mind will be turned to another of the interpretations, and to those who have suffered the devastation it gives and confirms the hopes of recovering again. We shall therefore make the purpose of the meaning for both as clear as possible. For the Jews, having spurned love for God, and holding the genuineness of piety toward Him in no account whatsoever, descended into polytheism and strange error and a life outside the law, and they built altars, they set up precincts to the works of their own hands, they brought rites and sacrifices to Astarte, to Chemosh, to Baal-peor, to the golden calves, and what is even more irrational than these, to them they dedicated songs of thanksgiving. For the wretched ones said out of their madness, "These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." But by such terrible impious acts they have forgotten themselves, sharpening against themselves the God who of old presided over and saved them, to whom they have become enemies, and have been placed in the portion of adversaries, assigning themselves to gods that are not so by nature, although Moses long ago cried out concerning God, that He is a jealous God, and a consuming fire, and that He would not endure those who chose to grieve Him.
Against the Pelagians 2.25

And again: "I will reestablish my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am Lord, that you may remember and be confounded and may no more open your mouth because of your confusion, when I shall be pacified toward you for all that you have done, says the Lord God." Thus it is clearly indicated by these divine words what was meant in another place by the statement "And though cleansing you he shall not make you innocent." Even the just, being restored to their former state after committing sin, do not dare open their mouth but say with the apostle, "I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God."
Commentary on Nahum

The Lord is patient and great in strength, and, cleansing, he will not make innocent. This is said more expressively in the Greek: καὶ ἀθῳῶν οὐκ ἀθῳώσει (and clearing he will not clear). And the sense is: he was indeed long patient with the crime of the Assyrians, and by the strength of his magnanimity bore their iniquities, calling them to repentance; but since, having despised the goodness of God, according to their impenitent heart they stored up for themselves wrath on the day of wrath, he who before was patient will by no means allow them to go away unpunished as though clean and innocent. Or certainly thus — since we wish at the same time to take what is said in a good sense —, he is patient who upholds all who are falling, and raises up those who are dashed down, who heals the troubled in heart and binds up their bruises, and great is his power, dissolving the enmities in the flesh, and not making the guilty innocent, since even he who applauds himself overmuch will be convicted of having been saved not by his own merit but by the mercy of God. For although he may say: Behold, I have served you so many years, and I have never passed over your command, yet since the Lord is good to all, and his mercies are over all his works; and all have sinned, and lack the glory of God, justified by him freely, he will hear: Or is your eye evil, because I am good? And so it will come about that in the very act by which he reproves and pardons, he allows no one to go away as innocent.

The Lord, in storm and whirlwind are his ways, and clouds are the dust of his feet. For storm and whirlwind the Seventy translated consummation and commotion, although where we have put in storm, and where in the Hebrew basupha is written, it can also be understood as in commotion. This signifies that at the end of the world all things will be moved, according to what is written in Haggai: Yet once more I too will move heaven and earth, sea and dry land; and when all things have been moved — so that they may believe the ways of the Lord, who says in the Gospel: I am the way, and the life, and the truth, and: When the Son of Man comes in the clouds, which in Isaiah are commanded not to rain rain upon the vineyard, and to which the truth of God reaches, as the psalmist says: Your truth even to the clouds —, then the clouds themselves too, namely the prophets and the souls of the saints, which before had been weighed down by their union with the flesh, will be lifted on high and become of a finer substance, and, brought down to be the footstool of God's feet, will minister among the angels in each of the lowest offices. For they will not be able to know the former and ancient things that pertain to the head. But another will take the clouds in the contrary sense, because they always trouble what is serene, and strive to veil the clear light of the sun and stars with their darkness, and because afterwards, subjected to the Lord's power, they are reduced to dust and to nothing, and the earth in them, which is fat, is dissolved.
Commentary on Nahum

The Lord's way is in destruction and in shaking, and clouds are the dust of his feet. As the Prophet is about to proclaim beforehand the capture of Nineveh for the comfort of those who have suffered, and to make clear to the wronged that it will be shaken down by God, he usefully recounts first the all-powerful nature of the divine, and that for it, when it chooses to accomplish anything whatsoever, there is nothing that resists, but rather everything follows easily, and what seems good to it will prevail, even if some earthly matter seems difficult for us and for those like us to accomplish. For the Jews thought that the Babylonians would be most difficult to capture, and possessed a hand so invincible, that not even if God wished it, could they be weak against their enemies. For I think the things dared by them cruelly and savagely throughout their whole country called them to this despair. Therefore, so that they might know that they will lie down without a struggle when the wrath of God rises up against them, and they will be captured, and very easily, he necessarily says, The Lord's way is in destruction and in shaking, and clouds are the dust of his feet. For if, he says, you should plan against some—for this is the way—it will surely run down upon them as in an earthquake. An earthquake and destruction are an invincible and altogether inescapable thing, and in addition to these, clouds flying like dust and covering the sky. And the Prophet seems to be bringing them to the remembrance of the flood that happened against the whole race of men in the time of Noah, for then God went forth, as it were, in destruction and in an earthquake against all, raising up clouds and, as the sacred scripture says, opening the floodgates of heaven, and inundating the world under heaven with irresistible rains.
AGAINST MARCION 4.20

If it is [Marcion's] Christ that is meant, he will not be stronger than the servants of the Creator. I would have been content with the examples I have shown you without adding anything further. But here a prediction of [Christ] walking on the water precedes his advent as well. The words of the psalm are, in fact, accomplished by Christ's crossing over the lake. "The Lord," says the psalmist, "is upon many waters." When he scatters its waves, Habakkuk's words are fulfilled where he says, "scattering the waters as he walks." When at his rebuke the sea is calmed, Nahum is also verified: "He rebukes the sea and makes it dry," referring to the winds that had disturbed the sea.
Commentary on Nahum

Rebuking the sea, and drying it up, and leading all the rivers to the desert. According to the letter, the power of God is described: since he is about to vindicate Israel against its adversaries, it is no great thing for him to destroy the Assyrians, whose majesty is such that he can even change the elements. Or certainly, since we have said once for all that the prophecy concerns the consummation of the world, take this too in the simple sense. When the consummation of the world comes, and heaven and earth pass away, the sea too and the rivers are dried up. But to me, as I read that passage in the psalms: This great and wide sea, there are creeping things without number, small animals with great. There the ships pass, that dragon which you formed to mock him, it seems worthy of the goodness and clemency of God to destroy by his threat all the bitterness and saltiness of the sea, and to humble the dragon that reigns in the waters, and to dry up the whirlpools of malice in which the small creeping things swim, of which there is no number; for the things that dwell with the dragon are not worthy of number. Leading the rivers also to the desert: all knowledge falsely so called, which, raising itself against God, uses the river of eloquence and volubility of words, and, rolling its swelling whirlpools, is borne headlong to the wonder of those who watch. Look at Plato, behold Demosthenes, and Tully too, philosopher and orator alike, and consider the chiefs of the heretics, among whom were Valentinus, Marcion, Bardesanes, Tatian, and you will have no doubt about the rivers. But all these the Lord Jesus will consume with the spirit of his mouth, and destroy with the illumination of his coming, and will lead to the deserts. And at the same time observe that, according to the title, which is inscribed The taking up of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite, rightly both is the world understood figuratively in Nineveh, and its sea and rivers of eloquence are dried up at the consummation.

Bashan has grown weak, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon has languished. LXX: Basanitis has been diminished, and Carmel, and the things of Lebanon that flourished have failed. Μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically), through Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon, a fertile region and planted mountains, the devastation of the Assyrian is shown, because he, once powerful and flourishing and ruling over very many nations, is to be laid waste when the Lord is angry. But we can also understand it of the consummation of the world, that all the powerful and noble, and those abounding in excessive wealth, suddenly perish, and it is said to them: Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? Moreover, according to the interpretation of the names, since Bashan sounds confusion and disgrace, we assert that at the consummation of the world, when the Lord comes, everything that is worthy of disgrace and blushing grows weak, and that not only are sins reduced to nothing, but also Carmel, which is interpreted knowledge of circumcision, and those who seem to themselves rich and flourishing in good works, tremble at the coming of Christ, and that the saying in the Gospel is fulfilled: When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on the earth? For as iniquity increases, the charity of very many will grow cold, and on account of these things the wrath of God will come.
Commentary on Nahum

The mountains were moved by him, and the hills were made desolate, and the earth trembled before his face, and the world, and all who dwell in it. LXX: The mountains were moved by him, and the hills were shaken, and the earth shrank back before his face, the universe and all who dwell in it. It can also be taken simply: that at the consummation of the world, when the Savior comes in his majesty, the mountains and hills, the world and the earth, and all things are moved. For if at his passion the sun fled, the rocks were split, the earth trembled, much more will all things be thrown into turmoil at his glory. But figuratively too the mountains and hills are to be understood as the lofty and powerful, who at the coming of the Lord will be cast down to the ground, and, deposed from their throne, will cleave to the pavement. The face for of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. Then too the earth will tremble, and the world and the universe will dread the face of the Lord, counting it the supreme torment and punishment that they will not dare to look on his face.
Commentary on Nahum

Before the face of his indignation who will stand, and who will resist in the wrath of his fury? LXX: From the face of his wrath who will endure, and who will resist in the wrath of his fury? In place of what we have put: And who will resist in the wrath of his fury? Symmachus translated more plainly: And who will endure the wrath of his fury? Therefore one will be found rarely, or not at all, who is not deserving of the wrath that rebukes. Nor will there be any soul that does not tremble at the judgment of God, since even the stars are not clean in his sight. Moreover, the Hebrew word iaccum, which Aquila and the Seventy translated will resist, let us transfer to that understanding of which it is said, in the second book of Kingdoms (2 Samuel) and in the first book of Chronicles, concerning the wrath of God, in the masculine gender. And no one doubts that there the wrath of God is understood as the devil, and the most wicked angels, who are sent to punish those who are worthy of wrath. So it will be hard to find, at the consummation of the world, one who, spotless and pure, dares to say: Behold, the prince of this world comes, and finds nothing in me, and stands against him with a free brow. But against the Assyrians it must be understood thus: that when the Lord comes in storm and whirlwind, drying up the empire of Babylon, which is interpreted sea, and overturning all its kingdoms, which are understood as rivers, and reducing to nothing its power and fertility, which μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically) are called Bashan and Carmel and the flower of Lebanon, and mountains and hills, and shaking the breadth of its empire, which is called the world, then no power will be able to resist God when he is angry and vindicating his people.

His indignation has been poured out like fire, and the rocks have been dissolved by him. LXX: His fury consumes principalities, and the rocks have been crushed by him. In place of what we have put, has been poured out, Aquila translated συνεχωνεύθη, that is, has been fused, Symmachus and Theodotion ἔσταξεν, that is, has dripped. Whether, then, the indignation of God has been fused like fire, or his fury has dripped in the likeness of a blaze, so that the hard hearts of men, which are called rocks, might be crushed and dissolved, the indignation of God is useful, which, long bearing our sins through patience, has scarcely ever been fused, and yet does not burst forth wholly into punishment, but will drip on us with a moderate heat. But if a drop of his indignation consumes the principalities, against whom we have the wrestling of battle, what would happen if the whole wrath of God were poured out on us? May Jesus grant that the heart of stone be taken away and changed in us into a heart of flesh, and that, its hardness softened, it may receive into itself the precepts of the Lord which are written: For a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise. And that you may know that what has been said sounds of the clemency of God, not of severity, learn from what follows.
Commentary on Nahum

Good is the Lord, and strengthening in the day of tribulation, and knowing those who hope in him. LXX: Sweet is the Lord to those who wait for him in the day of tribulation, and recognizing those who fear him. When he has begun to be angry with the nations and to lay waste kingdoms once most powerful, he will know those who are his, and will not overwhelm those at sea in one and the same storm. But let us understand the day of tribulation, according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), as the day of judgment, of which Isaiah wrote: Behold, the day of the Lord comes, incurable, of fury and of wrath, to make the world a desert and to destroy sinners out of it. Let us hope in the Lord, and through patience await his coming, so that when he comes we may experience him as good, not as a judge, and that he may recognize either those who hope in him or those who fear him. For the Lord knows those who are his.
Commentary on Nahum

And in a flood passing by he will make a consummation of its place, and darkness will pursue his enemies. LXX: And in a flood passing over he will make a consummation; darkness will pursue those rising up and his enemies. The Lord is patient and of great mercy, and he will not be angry to the end, nor will he be indignant forever; but when wickedness has grown upon the earth, and all flesh has corrupted its way, he will bring on a flood that is to pass through, not to remain forever. But he will make a consummation, or an end, of its place, that is, of the flood, so that, just as it is said of the impious man: And I passed by, and his place was not found, and: The way of the impious will perish, so the way of the flood may perish after the wrath of the Lord, with mercy alone appearing. This indeed can also be understood according to the history: when he has laid Israel waste, and has inundated the land of promise as if with a flood, he will make an end of the captivity, calling him back to his former dwellings. But on the contrary, darkness will pursue his enemies the Assyrians, who led the people into captivity. But what we have said of Israel and the Assyrians can be understood of the consummation of the world, and of the saints and of the persecutors, or the opposing powers: that God has mercy on the saints after his wrath; but as for the persecutors and their enemies, who have chosen darkness and not light, the very darkness that they chose will seize them; for they will be sent into the outer darkness: There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The word macoma, which we have translated "of its place", all have divided into two parts of speech, so that they turned ma into the preposition "from", that is, ἀπὸ, and interpreted coma as "rising up". Finally Aquila says ἀπὸ ἀνισταμένων, that is, "from those rising up"; the Seventy, "those rising up"; Theodotion, "for those rising up against him"; the Fifth edition, "from those rising up against him". Symmachus alone, agreeing with our translation, says: And in a flood passing over, he will make a consummation of its place. Some of our own interpret "those rising up and the enemies" as Marcion and all the old heretics, who dispute against the Creator.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 11

This, that according to the law, for example, the "adulterer or adulteress" was punished with present death: on account of this very thing, that he bore the penalty of his sin and paid the worthy punishments of the crime committed, what will there be after this that threatens vengeance to their souls, if they have transgressed in nothing else, if there is no other sin which condemns them, but they committed this alone and only then, when they were punished and bore the punishment of the law for this? "The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing"; for they received back their sin and the penalty of the crime is consumed. And therefore this kind of precept is found to be not cruel, as the heretics assert, accusing the law of God and denying that anything of humanity is contained in it, but full of mercy, for the reason that through it the people would be purged from their sins rather than condemned.
Commentary on Nahum

Moreover, since, having been taught by the Hebrews, we wish to follow their tradition too, and to set out for our own, that is, for Christians, an explanation of the history, it must be said: A twofold tribulation will not rise up, that is, the two tribes will not be captured by the Assyrians as the ten were captured. For while the Assyrians are still in the land of Judah, and like thorns embrace one another, glad and rejoicing, they will be consumed by the angel, when in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the enemy were slain. Beautifully, too, he compared the multitude of their army to a banquet of drunkards, and said that the banquet itself was not of roses, not of lilies, not of flowers, but like thorns embracing one another, which are always handed over to the fire and, like stubble full of dryness, are burned up by a slight blaze. But what follows: Out of you will go forth one plotting wickedness against the Lord, turning over transgression in his mind, they want it understood of Rabshakeh, because, having come forth from the Assyrians, he blasphemed God and wished to persuade the people to despair of the Lord's help and hand themselves over to the Assyrians, to serve not God but idols.
Commentary on Nahum

What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will make a consummation; a twofold tribulation will not rise up. LXX: What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will make a consummation, he will not avenge twice on the same thing in tribulation. Symmachus more plainly: They will not withstand the onset of a second distress; Theodotion: A second tribulation will not rise up. But according to tropology he is speaking against Marcion, of whom we spoke above, and against all the old heretics, who, inventing some good God or other, say that he is the one who will make the consummation of the world, and accuse the God of the law as if of cruelty, because he punishes many and inflicts torments for sins. What then, he says, are you plotting against the Lord? He himself who created the world will also make its consummation. But if he seems to you cruel, harsh and bloody, because he blotted out the human race in the flood, rained fire and sulphur upon Sodom and Gomorrah, drowned the Egyptians in the waves, and laid low the corpses of the Israelites in the desert, know that he exacted punishments in the present for this reason: that he might not punish forever. Surely what the prophets say is either true or false. If what they seem to say about his severity is true, they themselves have said: The Lord will not avenge twice on the same thing in tribulation. But if they are false, then this too is false that is said: A twofold tribulation will not rise up; false, therefore, is also the cruelty that is described in the law. But if it is true, as they will not be able to deny, since the prophet says: The Lord will not avenge twice on the same thing in tribulation, then those who have been punished are not punished afterward. But if they are punished afterward, Scripture lies, which it is impious to say. Therefore those who perished in the flood, and the Sodomites, and the Egyptians, and the Israelites in the wilderness received their evil things in their lifetime. Here someone may ask, if a believer caught in adultery is beheaded, what becomes of him afterward. For either he will be punished, and this saying is false: The Lord will not avenge twice on the same thing in tribulation, or he will not be punished, and it is something for adulterers to wish for, that by a short and swift penalty in the present they may escape eternal torments. To this we will answer that God, as he knows the measures of all things, so knows the measures of punishments too; that he is not forestalled by the sentence of a judge, nor is the power taken from him of exercising punishment on the sinner thereafter; and that a great sin is washed away by great and long-lasting torments. But if anyone has been punished, like him in the law who had cursed the Israelites, and him who had gathered wood on the sabbath, such men are not punished afterward, because a light fault has been compensated by the present punishment. The Hebrew expounded this passage thus: What do you think, O Assyrians, you who plot iniquity against the Lord, that he himself would consume the people of Israel, that is, the twelve tribes, to the point of extermination? A twofold tribulation will not rise up, that is, he will not hand over Judah and Jerusalem to you as he handed over the ten tribes and Samaria.
Commentary on Nahum

For as thorns embrace one another, so is their banquet of men drinking together; it will be consumed like stubble full of dryness. LXX: For even to their foundations they will be reduced into brambles, and like bindweed wound about it will be devoured, and like stubble full of dryness. The three distinctions which the Lord set down in the parable of the sowing, apart from the good soil, which bears fruit thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold, the prophet seems to me to unfold again: one, the seed that fell beside the way, another that fell among stones, and a third that fell among thorns; and the Apostle too, speaking of those who do not build well upon the foundation of Christ, indeed intimates this, that there are some who build wood, hay, stubble. Let us therefore refer the wood to what is now said: For even to their foundations they will be reduced to brambles. But the hay to what follows: And like bindweed that is wound about, it will be devoured. Moreover, the stubble is plainly referred to the stubble of which it is now said: And like stubble full of dryness. For this reason, then, the Lord will not avenge twice on the same thing, because the wickedness that had arisen in the authors of heresy will be consumed down to the foundation and to its roots. And if anyone among them seemed to have a pomp of words, that is, empty leaves that delight only the eye, he will be devoured like bindweed, which in Greek is called σμίλαξ, and will be consumed into nothing. Now bindweed is a plant like ivy, which commonly winds itself around vines and shrubs and creeps a long way. Whatever in them, too, seems to have the show of a crop, but has no ears and grains of wheat, will be handed over to the fire like stubble full of dryness. This is according to the Seventy. But according to the Hebrew, truly the alliances and close ties of the heretics are like thorns embracing one another, and their banquet and their mysteries, since they too say that they have the Lord's table, are a league of thorns, eating together and drinking together alike. For when, drunk from the vine of Sodom, they blaspheme against the Maker with rabid mouth, is it not a banquet of briars? Yet it will be consumed together with its authors, like stubble full of dryness.
Commentary on Nahum

For out of you will go forth one plotting wickedness against the Lord, turning over transgression in his mind. LXX: Out of you will go forth a thought against the Lord, most evil, thinking contrary things. Truly from the heretics will go forth a thought hostile to the Lord. Does it not seem to be wickedness and transgression against God to say, as Valentinus does, that the Creator was brought forth last, as if the abortion of an erring Wisdom? Is not the shamelessness of Basilides a thought against God, and the monstrous name ἄβραξας (Abraxas), which is set above the Lord the Maker?
Commentary on Nahum

Thus says the Lord: If they are complete, and so more numerous, even so they will be shorn, and he will pass through; I have afflicted you, and I will not afflict you any more; and now I will break his rod from your back, and I will burst your bonds. LXX: Thus says the Lord, reigning over many waters: and so they will be divided, and your report will not be heard any more; and now I will break his rod from you, and I will burst his bonds. According to the letter the sense is plain: Although, he says, the Assyrians are strong, and their might is increased by the number of all the nations, even so, as the angel lays waste, they are shorn. For just as the number of the hairs does not resist the sharp shears, so too the number of God's adversaries will be removed by an easy cutting down, and Asshur will pass through: either he will cease to exist, or, his army laid waste, he will return to his homeland, leaving you safe. And again the word is directed to Judah and Jerusalem: I have afflicted you, and I will not afflict you any more, not that he promises perpetual security, but only for that time, and from those enemies by whom it was then besieged.
Commentary on Nahum

But according to the LXX the sense is far different. For he still seems to be speaking against those to whom he had said above: What are you plotting against the Lord? and: Out of you will go forth a thought against the Lord, most evil, thinking contrary things. Thus, then, says the Lord, reigning over many waters, that is, over the powers, which are called the waters above the heavens, and which are commanded to praise the Lord, or else over the understandings and the wisdom and the teachings of God. For just as rivers will flow from the belly of the righteous man, and abundant springs unto eternal life, through the various and manifold meanings over which the word of the Lord rules, so the heresiarchs too have their own waters, over which they rule, and which first flowed from their spring. But what follows: And so they will be divided, can be understood either of the heavenly powers that serve God on high, in that each one is in its own office and ministry, or of the manifold variety of wisdom; lest, because he had said: Reigning over many waters, the number of meanings should be thought confused and undistinguished, but rather that each statement has meanings divided among themselves, and separate matters and its own ὑποθέσεις (subjects). For what is said: Your report will not be heard any more, is a rebuke against those who had thought things contrary to God: that, once the sophisms and snares by which the people of God was entangled have been exposed, their word may no longer run its course, nor be received by the peoples.
Commentary on Nahum

Finally he adds: And now I will break his rod, that is, the Assyrian's, from your back, and I will burst your bonds; either signifying his power by a metaphor, or else the rod with which he was trying to strike, and the bonds which he was preparing for the captives; although the siege of the shut-in multitude can also be taken for the bonds.
Commentary on Nahum

But this too, which he adds: And now I will break his rod from you, and I will burst your bonds, is said on behalf of the very ones against whom the threat is made, that they may by no means be beaten by the devil, nor be subject to him at whose instigation they had devised and fabricated such great things. Therefore his dominion over them will be broken, and the bonds by which the souls of sinners were bound will be burst by the word of God, saying to those who are in bonds: Go out.
Commentary on Nahum

And the Lord will command against you: It shall not be sown from your name any more. From the house of your god I will slay the graven and the molten image; I will make your grave, for you are without honor. LXX: And the Lord will command concerning you: It shall not be sown from your name any more. From the house of your god I will destroy the graven images and the molten images, I will make your grave, for they are swift; behold upon the mountains the feet of one who brings good news and announces peace. I have set down more from the Seventy translators for this reason, that the second περικοπὴ (pericope) could not be separated from the first. For where it says, for you are without honor, for which the Fifth edition put ὅτι ὑβρίσθης, the Seventy translated: for they are swift, which in the Hebrew reads chi calloth. But unless you refer "swift" to the feet of the following section, the sentence is left hanging. Therefore, according to my custom, I will sift first the history, and afterward the sense of the common edition. The Lord, he says, will command against you, O Asshur, so that what you are to suffer may not come by chance and without any judge, but you may suffer it at God's pronouncement. It shall not be sown from your name any more: for indeed Sennacherib, as soon as he had returned to Nineveh, was killed by his sons. Read Isaiah: and he was killed in the house of his god, which he had entered to worship. For this is what he says: From the house of your god I will slay: you will be punished from the place from which you hoped for help. The graven and the molten image will be your grave, so that amid the altars and the sacred couches the impious blood of one worshipping idols may be poured out.
Commentary on Nahum

But according to the Seventy translators, join what follows to what precedes: It shall not be sown, he says, from your name any more. By no means, O heretics, will the souls of the deceived take from your dogmas the names which they had previously invoked upon their lands, as is sung figuratively in the forty-eighth (49th) psalm. And this very cessation of sowing will profit you, a sowing which used to kill first the soul of the sower, then that of him in whom he sowed. The dogmas of errors, therefore, will die for you; and you too, who before seemed to yourself to be alive, will die to error, and, dead for your own good, you will have as your grave the idols which you used to worship. And so it will come about that from your breast, which before had been the temple of your god, whom you had feigned, all errors will be taken away. And these things will happen to you, who once used to think things contrary to the Lord, when the word of God, which always ascends upon the mountains, that is, into lofty and sublime souls, has come swiftly to you, and, having trodden down the waves of your former errors and brought them to calm, has restored to you the peace and the sense of faith. Pardon my prolixity; for in following both the history and the tropology I cannot take in both briefly, especially since I am tormented by the variety of the translations, and am sometimes compelled, against my conscience, to weave together the sequence of the common edition.
City of God 18.31

The prophet Nahum (or, better, God speaking through him) says, "I will destroy the graven and molten thing; I will make it your grave. Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that brings peace. O Judah, keep your festivals and pay your vows, for it shall no longer be that they may pass into disuse. It is completed, it is consumed, it is taken away. He is come up that breathes into your face and rescues you from tribulation." Anyone who knows the Gospels will recognize who it was that came up from hell and breathed the Holy Spirit into the face of Judah, that is, into the face of his Jewish disciples. The words about the festivals are, of course, a reference to the New Testament, in which festivals are so spiritually renewed that they can never "pass into disuse." The rest of the prophecy too we see realized in that the gospel brought about the destruction of "graven and molten things," that is, the idols of the false gods, consigned now to the oblivion of the grave.
Commentary on Nahum

Behold upon the mountains the feet of him who brings good tidings and announces peace. Celebrate, O Judah, your feasts, and pay your vows, for Belial will no more pass through you; he has wholly perished. For a little while I shall put off the LXX translators, because among them the very sections are also confused by the variety of their translation. And when I have briefly set out the history, I shall temper their edition with my own words. It is written in the book of Chronicles that while Sennacherib was besieging them, they could not keep the Passover in the first month; but when his army had been slain by the angel, and his flight and death had been announced, they celebrated the day of the Passover in the second month with the greatest festivity. What he says, then, is this: O Judah, you who reign in Jerusalem, do not be anxious, now that your enemy has been killed in the temple of his god. Behold, a messenger comes to you, running over the mountains and hills, and as if from a lofty watchtower announcing from afar that Sennacherib is dead and the world freed from his rule. Celebrate your festivals; pay the vows for the death of your enemy which you promised to God; never again will the transgressor and ἀποστάτης (apostate) pass through you, for this is what Belial means. He has wholly perished, that is, both the army and the king and the empire of the Assyrians have utterly fallen. And this indeed according to the letter. But according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy) it is said to the Church, it is said to the souls that confess the Lord, that the devil, who formerly laid you waste and pressed you down under a most heavy yoke, has perished in the idols and with the idols which he had fashioned: Celebrate your feasts and pay your vows to God, singing continually with the angels, for never again will Belial pass through you, of whom the Apostle also says: What fellowship has Christ with Belial? Because, Nineveh being overthrown, he has wholly perished.
Commentary on Nahum

If ever there has been a most grievous persecution, such as under Valerian and Decius and Maximian, and the vengeance of the Lord has appeared upon his adversaries, let us say to the Church: LXX: Celebrate, O Judah, your feasts, pay your vows, for they will never again add to pass through into oldness; it is fulfilled, it is consummated; he has gone up breathing into your face, rescuing you from tribulation. I have said once already that according to the variety of the translation the sections themselves are also divided differently, and that the sense of the Hebrew translation cannot agree with the sections. Therefore what is now said is of this kind: O man of the Church, since from the name of your adversaries there shall be no more sowing, and their rod is broken, and their bonds are torn apart, and he has come who should announce peace to you, celebrate your feasts, not in wine and banquets, as the carnal Jews suppose, but in spiritual delights and the torrent of pleasure. O Judah, pay your vows, for never again will enemies pass through you to lead you into oldness, that is, who wish you to bear the image of the old man. For what is old grows aged, and what grows aged is near to perishing: the world is fulfilled, the adversary is consumed. Christ has come to you, who earlier had breathed into your face when he formed you from the clay, and after the resurrection too, breathing into the face of the apostles, said: Receive the Holy Spirit; he it is who frees you from tribulation. For when Nineveh is laid waste and the world passes away, tribulation too will pass away.

n: Face, O Juda. Septuagint, "who blows on thy face, (Genesis ii. 7.) freeing from misery." Here St. Jerome's Greek copy ends the chapter. (Haydock) --- Watch. Behold Nabopolassar is about to attack thy enemies. Some think that Nahum addresses Ninive ironically. (Calmet) --- Nabuchodonosor wasted all the environs, and then took the city (Worthington) after his other conquests. (Calmet) --- But his father is here denoted. (Haydock)Ver. 2. Pride, &c. He hath punished Jacob for his pride; and therefore Ninive must not expect to escape. Or else, rendering the pride of Jacob means rewarding, that is, punishing Ninive for the pride they exercised against Jacob. (Challoner) --- After the Assyrians had seized the ten tribes, they became more insolent, and are therefore punished. (Worthington) --- The haughty Phul, &c., had invaded the Israelites, and had taken them into captivity. This God will now resent, (Calmet) though he justly chastised his people by them. (Haydock)Ver. 3. Mighty men. He speaks of the Chaldeans and Medes sent to destroy the Ninivites. (Challoner) --- This is the common opinion. Yet it seems rather that the Ninivites are designated, as they were asleep and stumbled, &c. (Calmet) --- Stupified. That is, they drive on furiously, like men intoxicated with wine. (Challoner) --- Hebrew, "the fir-tree shall be shaken," or poisoned. Psalm cxix. 4. Septuagint read better, (Calmet) "their horsemen shall be in a hurry, or in confusion." (Haydock) --- The armour was kept very shining, and the soldiers of Cyrus were clothed in purple, like himself. (Xen. iii.) --- Yet this availed nothing, while the men were asleep or confounded. (Calmet)Ver. 4. Streets. The Ninivites are disordered at the enemy's approach. (St. Jerome)Ver. 5. Muster. Literally, " remember" (Haydock) the ancient heroes, Salmanasar, &c. (Calmet) --- Stumble, by running hastily on. (Challoner) --- Prepared to defend the city. (Haydock) --- All this represents a city surprised. It attempts to defend itself; but God renders all efforts vain. (Calmet)Ver. 6. Gates; floodgates or channel of the Tigris overflowing, chap. i. 8. --- Temple. Septuagint," palace." Ver. 7. Soldier. Hebrew hutsab, (Haydock) "the station" or guard; the queen, or the statue of the idol, with the women (Calmet) who prostituted themselves in its honour. (Sanct. xxxi.) --- Ninive and its dependances are taken. (Grotius)Ver. 8. Waters: multitudes, (Apocalypse xvii. 15.) and riches; (Calmet) or the flood bursting upon them makes them flee. (Haydock) --- The citizens run away when the enemy had made a breach, as water does when the dam is broken down; and though some more valiant will exhort them to tarry, they will not succeed, nor save the city. (Worthington)Ver. 10. Kettle. In mourning they blacken their face. (Tav. Perse.)Ver. 11. Lions. The kings of Assyria had plundered various nations, (Haydock) and had brought the spoils to Ninive. But all shall be lost. (Worthington) --- These princes followed no law but their own will. --- The lion, Nabopolassar, or his son: though it seems rather to relate to the Assyrian monarchs. (Calmet)Ver. 13. Chariots. Septuagint, "multitude." Some wild beasts were thus suffocated in their dens. (Theodoret) --- More, like that of the impious Rabsaces, 4 Kings xviii. 17. (Calmet)

f: Catechetical Lecture 17:12

He imparted the fellowship of this Holy Spirit to the apostles, for it is written, "When he had said that, he breathed upon them, and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained.' " This was the second breathing (the first had been impaired by willful sins)2 to fulfill the Scripture: "One who has been delivered from affliction has come up panting into your presence." He has been delivered from Hades. For it was after his resurrection, according to the gospel, that he breathed on them. He gives the grace at this time, and he will lavish it more abundantly. He says to them, "I am ready to give it to you even now, but the vessel cannot yet hold it. Accept for the time the grace of which you are capable, but look forward to yet more." "But wait here in the city" of Jerusalem "until you are clothed with power from on high." Receive it in part now; then you will be clad in its fullness. For he who receives often has the gift only in part, but he who is clothed is entirely covered by his garment. Fear not, he says, the weapons and darts of the devil, for you will possess the power of the Holy Spirit. But be mindful of our recent admonition, that the Holy Spirit is not divided, but only the grace he bestows.
Commentary on Nahum

He has come up who will scatter before your face, keeping the siege; watch the way, strengthen the loins, make your power very strong, for as the Lord has repaid the pride of Jacob, so the pride of Israel, because the ravagers have scattered them and have corrupted their branches. I am compelled by necessity to steer the course of my discourse between history and allegory, as between rocks and crags with shipwreck threatening, and to take care that it does not suddenly strike. For indeed, according to the fables of the poets: Scylla holds the right side, implacable Charybdis the left; if we flee the rocks, we run into the deep; if we avoid the twisting whirlpools, we are carried onto the rocks. The Lord is my witness that in all that I discuss according to the Hebrew I do not speak from my own sense, which is the charge laid against the false prophets, but follow the exposition of the Hebrews, by whom I was taught for no short time, and I am bound simply to point out to my readers what I have learned. Certainly it will be at the reader's discretion, when he has run through both, to judge which he ought rather to follow. Now therefore the discourse is turned to Nineveh — and it is above all on this account that the prophets are obscure, that suddenly, while one thing is being treated, the person is changed to others —, and it is said to her: Nebuchadnezzar has come up against you to besiege you, to lay waste the fields before your face, to pursue the farmers, to ravage the countryside, and to hold you yourself shut in as well. Since, then, war threatens you, behold, I the prophet now rejoicing foretell it: watch carefully and look, and observe what is coming upon you. Strengthen the loins, that is, gird yourself; make your power very strong, that is, gather armies, for as the Lord avenged Judah for the pride of Sennacherib, when his army was slain in Judea and he himself was also murdered by his own sons, so will he avenge Israel, that is, the ten tribes which are held in possession by Nineveh. For the Assyrians laid waste and overthrew both, Judah and Israel, and, under the metaphor of a vine, corrupted the branches of both.
Commentary on Nahum

LXX: Watch the way, hold the loin, be strengthened in strength exceedingly, for the Lord has turned away the insolence of Jacob, as the insolence of Israel, because those who shake out have shaken them out, and have demolished their branches. Three things are commanded to Judah. First, that he watch the way and look carefully at the road by which he is to walk, according to what is written in Jeremiah: Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths, and see which is the good way, and walk in it, so that when we have stood in many ways, we may come to that way which says: I am the way. Next it is said to him that he hold the loin, that is, that after choosing the way he mortify his body and bring it into subjection, lest, preaching to others as a king and master, he himself be found reprobate. It would take long now to tell how the strength of the devil is above all in the loins, and how the promise is made to David: Of the fruit of your loin I will set upon your throne, and that saying of the Apostle: For he was still in the loin of his father Abraham, Levi was, when Melchizedek went to meet Abraham. And how John is girded with a leather girdle, and how the disciples are commanded by the Savior: Let your loins be girded. And the Apostle to the Ephesians: Stand therefore, having your loins girded in truth; for although ἄσκησις (ascetic discipline) and continence of life avail very much toward the mortifying of the loins, yet nothing so mortifies them as the knowledge of the truth. Hence it is said: Gird your loins in truth. For if Christ is the truth, he who has believed in Christ with his whole mind has mortified his loins in Christ. Thirdly it is commanded: be strengthened in power exceedingly. You have chosen, he says, the way; you have held the loin; take up power, so that you may fight with the enemies.
Commentary on Nahum

It is finished, it is taken away; he has come up breathing into your face, delivering from affliction. As it was already fixed, and in every way and altogether about to happen that Nineveh must be destroyed, he says that it is finished, indicating by this its coming to an end, as it were. And indeed also that it is taken away, that is, that it has been cut off completely and utterly destroyed. And very well indeed he says "he has come up" concerning Cyrus, signifying something emphatic, I think, such as the prophet Jeremiah also said about him, foretelling what would happen in due time to Nineveh: "A lion has come up from his den, a destroyer of nations has set out, and has gone forth from his place, to make your land a desolation, and your cities shall be laid waste, so that none shall dwell in them." For like a wild beast leaping upon Nineveh, he devoured those in it. But to them he was a terrible and relentless enemy, and became unyielding in his wrath, but to those of Israel he was breathing into their face and delivering from affliction, that is, releasing them from their unusual servitude, loosing their bonds, recovering them as captives, by sending them home, and also commanding that the divine temple be rebuilt for them.
Commentary on Nahum

And lest perhaps you lose confidence, a reason is given you for hoping: The Lord, he says, has turned away the insolence of Jacob, as the insolence of Israel; which is ambiguous: for either the Lord has turned away the insolence of Jacob himself, with which he did injury to others, or he has turned away the insolence which Jacob endured from others. But it seems better to me that the insolence which Jacob used to do to others has been turned away by the Lord. For it is not of such great virtue to endure an injury done by others as it is of the Lord's grace to be calm, gentle and tranquil, unable to do injury. It is asked how the injury of Jacob was turned away, as that of Israel too had been turned away: after Jacob wrestled with the angel, he was found worthy to receive the name of Israel, and because he saw God, he ceased to do injury. As therefore Israel, sense or a man seeing God, and ever thinking of God, does not know how to do injury, so all wantonness and insolence has been turned away from Jacob, that is, from the supplanter, from him who, still set in the contest, supplants his enemies. And that we may know how injury is taken in the bad sense, Solomon is witness, saying: Insolent eyes, an unjust tongue. And how, according to both understandings, the injury has been turned away from Jacob which had earlier been turned away from Israel, the following words make plain: Because those who shake out have shaken them out, and have demolished their shoots, or have corrupted them. The angels, he says, of each one, who daily see the face of the Father, have shaken out whatever dust had clung to Jacob and Israel. Hence Peter's feet too are washed. And through the prophet it is said: Shake off the dust, and arise, O Jerusalem. The disciples too are commanded by the Savior: Shake off the dust of your feet. And in the psalms it is written: As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the sons of the shaken out. So the mind prompt to insolence has been turned away from the true Jacob and from the true Israel, because whatever had been earthly in them, and compacted of the lower dregs, has been shaken out and cleansed by the ministering angels, or by admonishers and teachers, who not only shook them out, but also scattered the vices, which soothe the senses with pleasure only for the present, and which are like shoots and branches that are full of leaves without fruit, as the Lord says: Every branch that abides in me and bears fruit, my Father cleanses, that it may bear more fruit; but what does not abide in me and does not bear fruit, my Father will cut off and cast into the fire.
Commentary on Nahum

Watch the road, brace your loins, be exceedingly courageous in your strength, because the Lord has turned away the insolence of Jacob, as the insolence of Israel. To those about to go very soon into Judea, and intending to go home, he necessarily adds that it is needful for the future both to watch the road and brace their loins, that is to be ready and prepared for the toils of the journey, and to be courageous against all hesitation, and to be seen to love being superior to long distances, using invincible eagerness for this. A sign of readiness is to have one's loins, as it were, well-ordered and girded. And indeed our Lord Jesus Christ says to the holy apostles, or rather to all who believe in him, "Let your loins be girded." For the posture is that of a traveler, and is most especially fitting for those who preach the divine gospel, and have their feet most ready for this. Therefore, he says, brace your loins, instead of, be prepared and, as it were, ready for a journey. For the Lord has turned away, he says, the insolence of Jacob as the insolence of Israel. Observe again in these words the distinction that is necessarily introduced. For by Jacob he means those who dwelt in Samaria, that is the ten tribes, over whom reigned those from the tribe of Ephraim and Manasseh, who came from Joseph, who was from Jacob; but by Israel he names those in Jerusalem, I mean Judah and Benjamin. And since, when Sennacherib had sacked Samaria, Jerusalem was not captured, as God at that time defended it and destroyed the Assyrian by the hand of an angel; and Cyrus released not only the captives from Samaria who had been carried away to Nineveh, but also those from Jerusalem, when Nebuchadnezzar had captured the land; the Prophet necessarily says that the Lord turned away the insolence of Jacob as the insolence of Israel. And by insolence he means slavery or servitude.
Commentary on Nahum

The shield of his mighty men is fiery, the men of the army are in scarlet; fiery are the reins of the chariot in the day of his preparation, and the charioteers have been lulled to sleep. They have been thrown into confusion on the roads; the four-horse chariots have been dashed together in the streets. Their appearance is like torches, like lightnings running to and fro. He will remember his mighty men; they will fall on their roads; swiftly they will go up to her walls, and a shelter will be prepared. The gates of the rivers have been opened, and the temple has been torn down to the ground, and the soldier has been led away captive, and her handmaids were driven along, moaning like doves, murmuring in their hearts. LXX: The arms of his power from men, mighty men mocking in fire, the reins of their chariots in the day of their preparation, and the horsemen will fear in the outgoings; and the chariots will be confounded and will be dashed together in the streets. Their appearance is like torches of fire, and like lightnings running to and fro, and their nobles will be remembered, and they will flee in the days, and they will grow weak on their way, and they will hasten to the walls, and they will prepare their bulwarks; the gates of the cities have been opened, and the royal things have fallen, and the substance has been uncovered; and she herself was going up, and her handmaids were being led like doves speaking in their hearts. According to the history the sequence continues against Nineveh, and the army of the Babylonians coming against her is described. And as for his saying, Fiery reins of the chariots: by the burning thongs he signifies the speed of those making ready, and the pomp, as it were of ἐπισκευῆς (of equipment), of those preparing themselves for battle is recounted. And the Scripture is woven together in a mingled way, now about what Israel once suffered, now about what the Assyrian did, now about what the Babylonians carry out against the Assyrians. It is not, therefore, he says, surprising if they come so swiftly to lay waste, since the charioteers and mighty men, either of Israel before or of the Assyrians afterward, had been lulled to sleep.
Commentary on Nahum

Now let us come to the Seventy translators. Those who shake out, who shook out Jacob and Israel and scattered their shoots, also broke the arms which they had been accustomed to have while they were insolent, and with which they had oppressed all the weak; and they did not do this only, but they also destroyed in fire the mighty men who were mocking. Consider whether you can call the mighty men mocking in fire the opposing powers, which serve the fiery darts of the devil, which, mighty and once mocking Jacob and Israel in fire, had chariots and horses, by which they were borne, urged on, into war in the day of their preparation. The reins of these chariots, then, and the horsemen will be thrown into confusion on the roads and will be dashed together in the streets, when, Jacob and Israel having been healed by the enlightening of the Lord, both the demons and those who serve their will shall be overthrown by the Lord. We can understand these things of his first coming, when the mighty men and the drivers of the chariots and the horsemen said: What have we to do with you, son of David? Have you come before the time to torment us? But since we have once taken the prophecy against Nineveh as concerning the consummation of the world, it is better for us to say that the arms of the devil's power are then taken away from men, and his mighty ministers, who mocked men in fire. For all their hearts are adulterers, like an oven; and we may say that the bonds too by which the captives were led into vices, and the riders of the chariots, are loosed. For the horsemen will fear in the outgoings, that is, in the consummation of the world, and they will be confounded, and the chariots will be dashed together in the streets; for although broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, yet, under the pressure of a time cut short, they will not be able to find a straight road; but they will be dashed against one another, and none the less they will breathe out their old fury, and like lightnings they will run to and fro hither and thither. I saw, says the Lord, Satan like lightning falling from heaven.
Commentary on Nahum

And returning again to the order of the description, he says: So great is the multitude of those coming that the column on the march is mingled together and cannot be told apart. The four-horse chariots themselves too, while they cannot find a way, are dashed against one another in the streets because of the multitude. The appearance of the Babylonians is like torches, like lightnings running to and fro, so that they terrify their adversaries by the sight before they lay them low with the sword.
Commentary on Nahum

Then Asshur will remember his mighty men and will look for those who fell on the roads, and he will swiftly go up the walls of Nineveh, and because of the very long siege he will prepare shelters to ward off the heat.
Commentary on Nahum

And when the devil and all his nobles have understood this, they will remember the consummation which had long ago been foretold, and they will flee in the days. For they will by no means move about in the nights, but as the day grows bright the darkness will be put to flight, and they will grow weak on the way, not making progress nor fulfilling their endeavors, and they will hasten to the walls. For so great a terror of the coming Lord will seize them, and so feeble will they be for resisting, that they will flee to the bounds of the world, by which the world is shut in and encircled as by walls, and they will prepare themselves to resist. Just as, if someone flees an enemy, not daring to resist him, when he has come into a solitary place, if perhaps the foe follows, he is compelled by necessity to fight back.
Exposition of the Christian Faith 3.14.115-16

But is this the only place we read of "substance"? Has it not also been said in another passage: "The gates of the cities are broken down, the mountains are fallen, and his substance is revealed"? What, does the word mean something created here also? Some, I know, are accustomed to say that the substance is substance in money. Then, if you give this meaning to the word, the mountains fell in order that someone's possessions of money might be seen. But let us remember what mountains fell, those, namely, of which it has been said, "If you shall have faith as a grain of mustard seed you shall say to this mountain, 'Be removed, and be cast into the sea!' " By mountains, then, are meant high things that exalt themselves.
Commentary on Nahum

But what does it profit to build a house unless the Lord has built it? What does it help to shut the gates which the Lord unbars? The gates of Nineveh have been opened, which had a multitude of citizens like rivers, and the temple, that is, her kingdom, has been destroyed, and the soldier has been led away captive, that is, all have been led into Babylon. But by the handmaids of Nineveh understand, by a metaphor, the lesser cities and villages and forts. Or certainly the captive women will be driven along before the faces of the victors; and so great will be the terror that their grief will not even break out into sobbing and wailing, but they will moan silently within themselves and with a dark murmur swallow their tears, after the manner of cooing doves. These things according to the Hebrew tradition.
Commentary on Nahum

But while they are thinking this, all the things which had been held and possessed by them will be brought out into the open, and the gates which they had shut will be opened, and their kingdoms will fall, and the substance, that is, the riches, will be uncovered. But the substance of the world itself and all her handmaids, after they have subjected themselves to Christ and have begun to serve him, will be led glad and rejoicing, and believing from the inmost heart of confession, so that they are compared to the cleanness of doves, they will murmur or speak in their hearts. And then will be fulfilled what is said in the sixty-seventh (68th) psalm of the victory of the Savior: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.
Commentary on Nahum

But since we have once said that Nineveh is the beautiful one, that is, the world, let us see what the pool of the world is. Scripture does not say that the waters of Nineveh are like the waters of the sea, nor like the waters of rivers, nor like the waters of springs, nor like the waters of wells, but like the waters of a pool, so that, just as in Jeremiah the people is rebuked which forsook the fountain of living water and dug for itself broken cisterns that cannot hold water, so in Nineveh too all those waters are such as have fallen from heaven and, leaving their ancient height, have slipped down to the depths. For all the dogmas of this world which are outside the fountain of the Church and the sealed garden, and cannot say: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God, nor are of those waters which above the heavens praise the name of the Lord, though they seem great, are nevertheless small and shut in within a narrow bound. And let it not disturb anyone that we take the pool in the bad sense, when that pool to which Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, is commanded to go up is taken in the good sense. For there it is said with an addition: The pool of the aqueduct, and the pool of the fuller, which is accustomed to wash away filth and to cleanse the stains of garments. And because it is set on high, the prophet is therefore commanded to go up to it and, in meeting the king, to promise victory over the two burnt firebrands. There follows: Fleeing, they did not stand, namely the inhabitants of Nineveh. First, indeed, they ought not to have fled from God; then, even if they had fled, they ought at some time to stand. For there is a great difference between him who fled and stood, and him who, fleeing, never stood. For he who stands has ceased to flee; he who does not stand has gone forward in perpetual flight. In so great a crowd of those fleeing, therefore, there was no one who looked back and did repentance and heard the Lord speaking: Return to me, O sons, returning, and I will heal your bruises. Hence the saint too says in the psalms: Flight has perished from me. I think that this very thing is also signified by the mystery of leprosy, concerning which it is said in Leviticus: When the leper has been separated by the priest outside the camp, if the leprosy has stood still, the man is clean, and he who had been cast out as a leper is cleansed and returns to the camp and dwells among the people. But if, he says, the leprosy has spread, that is, has not stood still but has grown and made progress in evil and changed the color of its former health, then the leprosy is most plainly proved by him who has the knowledge of inspecting and purging leprosy. But we too are commanded by the true Solomon to dwell in Jerusalem and never to go out from it. And if what was formerly subject to us flees from us and goes to the Philistines, let us not go out of the walls of our city nor follow the footsteps of the fugitives; lest, while we wish to save those who flee, we ourselves perish; but rather let us let them go, that the dead may bury their dead, and, while we may, let us pluck out and cut off from ourselves the eye, the hand and the foot that cause us to stumble.
Commentary on Nahum

And Nineveh: like a pool of waters are her waters, but they have fled. Stand, stand, and there is none who turns back; plunder the silver, plunder the gold, and there is no end of riches from all the desirable vessels. LXX: And Nineveh: like a pool of waters are her waters, and they, fleeing, did not stand, and there was none who looked back; they were plundering the silver, they were plundering the gold, and there was no end of her adornment; she has been weighed down above all the vessels of her concupiscence. It is plain that, when the cities of Nineveh — which Scripture calls her daughters — have been led into captivity, Nineveh herself, who had nourished such great peoples that they were compared to the waters of pools, has a useless multitude, since there is no one to resist and to bear the onslaught of the Babylonians rushing in. For she had peoples who only fled, and while their mother cried out: Stand, stand, shut the gates, mount the walls, fight back against the enemy, there was no one who turned back, no one who looked back to his mother, but all, turning their backs, deserted the city as plunder for the enemy. Hence it is said to the Babylonians, since those have fled: Plunder the silver, and make spoil by a sudden ravaging of the wealth gathered over so long a time. For there is no end of the riches, the furniture and the vessels which are stored in Nineveh, nor can you carry off as much as she offers herself to be plundered.
Commentary on Nahum

And as for what is said: They were plundering the silver, they were plundering the gold, and there was no end of her adornment: she has been weighed down above all the vessels of her concupiscence, it is said of the waters of Nineveh, and of those fleeing who had fled and did not stand, nor was there one who looked back; and who, not content only to have fled and not to have looked back, were plundering the silver besides, whatever eloquence was seen in the world; they were plundering the gold, whatever was splendid in the way of maxims in the learning of the age, in order to adorn Nineveh, in order to compose their dogmas with every flower of thoughts and words. Because of this Nineveh has been weighed down above all the vessels of her concupiscence; for the more she had a great possession of gold and silver and varied furniture, which was heavy, the more she herself was weighed down, since she loved heavy things. Hence also iniquity in Zechariah sits upon a talent of lead, and the Egyptians, who were heavy with sins, sank in the sea like lead. And in the person of the sinner it is said in the psalm: Like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me. And Peter, who before, being light, trod the waves with suspended step, after he was weighed down by unbelief and was being swallowed by the billows, is lifted up by the hand of the Lord.
Commentary on Nahum

She has been scattered and torn and rent apart, and the heart is melting, and there is a loosening of the knees and a failing in all the kidneys, and the faces of all are like the blackness of a pot. LXX: A shaking out, a shaking out again, and a boiling up, and a breaking of heart and a loosening of knees, and pains upon every loin, and the faces too of all like the scorching of a pot. Under the metaphor of a captive woman, Nineveh is described as scattered, torn, rent: her heart melting, her knees loosened, and her kidneys broken, and the faces of all her inhabitants, through terror of the enemy and the greatness of their fear, appear scorched like pots, wasted, and disfigured with pallor. Moreover, according to the LXX we must understand at a higher level what shaking out, shaking out again signifies.
